title: The Black Death (1347–1351)
hookLine: a third of Europe dies; Jews are scapegoated, and Pope Clement VI condemns the killings
last: THE LOVE THAT MOVES THE SUN.

lines: A RUMOR FASTER THAN THE SICKNESS.
cards: A rumor travels faster than the sickness. In town after town along the trade roads, people are dying in their houses, and nobody can say why. Then someone says the wells have been poisoned.
Someone else says who did it: the Jews. In some towns, Jewish families who had lived beside their Christian neighbors are driven out, or burned. The sickness keeps coming anyway.
Today, that terrible season, told honestly, and one voice that refused the lie.

teach.b: First, the sickness. A plague swept across Europe. Households were lost, and some towns couldn't bury their dead fast enough.
Nobody understood how it spread, and fear went looking for a cause it could see. Second, the blame. In towns along the Rhine and elsewhere, Jewish communities were accused of poisoning wells.
Mobs, and sometimes town councils, killed many of them. This happened in Christian towns, at the hands of Christians. The Church remembers it, and does not excuse it.
Third, the pope. Clement the Sixth, living in Avignon, issued decrees against the killings.
His argument rested on plain evidence: Jews were dying of the plague like everyone else, and it was striking places where no Jews lived at all, so the accusation made no sense.
He ordered the clergy to protect Jews, and threatened with excommunication anyone who harmed them. His words did not stop every mob. But they named the lie.
Fourth, the Gospel's own refusal. In John's Gospel, the disciples see a man born blind and ask, in the Douay-Rheims: "who hath sinned, this man, or his parents, that he should be born blind?"
Jesus answers: "Neither hath this man sinned, nor his parents."

He refuses to turn suffering into blame, even with it right in front of him. In a Lenten liturgy of repentance, Pope John Paul the Second asked forgiveness for sins Christians had committed against the Jewish people.
Remembering the plague years honestly is part of that.

how: The Catholic Church remembers sins committed by Christians against the Jewish people in documents and acts of repentance, such as the Day of Pardon liturgy under Pope John Paul II, and Catholic teaching since the Second Vatican Council rejects blaming Jews collectively.

games.q: you're the pope. towns are killing Jews, blaming them for the plague. what do you do?
o: stay silent; the towns are frightened.
say the evidence proves the accusation false, and order protection.
wait for the plague to end and see.
games.why: Clement the Sixth pointed out that Jews were dying too and that the plague struck where no Jews lived, and he threatened excommunication for those who harmed them.

practice: Bring to mind people who have been blamed for a sickness, in history or in the news, and hold them one at a time; then notice, gently, whether any of that blame has ever lived in you, without arguing with it.
If you pray, bring them to God in your own words, or hold Jesus's answer, neither hath this man sinned; if not, simply wish them safety.

wordCard.voice: Clement. The pope who condemned the killing of Jews blamed for the plague, pointing out that Jews were dying of it too. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: no scapegoats. When fear asks who, the truer question is what happened. Day eight hundred twenty-one, done.
